 3          Tesla is an automotive and clean energy company, which undertook the development of a

 4   lithium refinery on a 1,200-acre site in Robstown, Texas (“Project”). Tesla approached Bedeschi,

 5   a Florida-based company, to provide material-handling equipment and services for the Project.

 6          On January 20, 2023, Petitioner and Respondents entered into the “General Terms and

 7   Conditions for Procurement of Production Equipment and Services” (“GTC”). In the GTC, Tesla

 8   and Bedeschi agreed to certain terms governing the parties’ relationship and future purchase orders.

 9          After several rounds of negotiation, the Parties executed a Purchase Order in which

11   be the first lithium refinery in the United States. After failing to timely deliver Tesla’s equipment

12   under the parties’ contract, Tesla notified Bedeschi that it was in default. Following the notification

13   of default, Bedeschi improperly raced to the courthouse and, on November 15, 2024, filed a lawsuit

14   against Tesla in violation of the GTC’s provisions on confidentiality and arbitration. The same day,

15   Bedeschi filed a Demand for Arbitration.

16          On November 11, 2025, Bedeschi filed its Statement of Claims. Bedeschi alleged claims

17   against Tesla for breach of contract, quantum meruit, violations of the Prompt Pay Act, and sought

18   a foreclosure of lien. Tesla counterclaimed for breach of contract and sought declaratory relief that

19   the lien is unenforceable.

20          Arbitrator Barry Baskin, a California licensed attorney and former California judge residing

21   in this jurisdiction, was appointed by JAMS. Between January 26-28, 2026, the Arbitrator

22   conducted the arbitration hearing (“Hearing”) in Austin, Texas. 1 On April 30, 2026, the Arbitrator

23   issued the Interim Award. Following denial of a motion for reconsideration, the Arbitrator issued

24   the Final Award, which adopted the Interim Award and was well in excess of $75,000. The

13                                      FACTUAL BACKGROUND

14          Tesla seeks vacatur of the Final Arbitration Award (which adopted the Interim Award

15   (collectively, “Award”), under 9 U.S.C. § 10 because the Arbitrator exceeded his authority and

16   showed manifest disregard of the law. The Award rests on a foundational error, which treated

17   Tesla’s termination of a Purchase Order as though it were a termination of the parties’ General

18   Terms and Conditions. The Award then completely ignores the parties’ contract and substitutes in

19   its place common-law substantial-performance principles, misapplies Texas Property Code

20   § 53.286 to void the parties’ agreement, and awards fees and costs that are barred by applicable

21   law. Because the Award ultimately contradicts the Arbitrator’s own factual findings on dispositive

22   facts, rewrites and largely ignores the parties’ agreement, and wholly ignores that law, it exceeds

23   the scope of the Arbitrator’s delegated authority and should be vacated.

24          As background, Tesla and Bedeschi entered into the General Terms and Conditions for

25   Procurement of Production Equipment and Services, under which Tesla could issue purchase orders

26   for production equipment and services on January 20, 2023. The GTC provides that the general

27   terms therein remain in effect until terminated by mutual agreement or by one of the termination

28   mechanisms specifically enumerated.
                                                         5
         Case 5:26-cv-07249         Document 1        Filed 07/14/26     Page 6 of 15



 1          More specifically, the GTC authorizes Tesla to terminate for material breach without

 2   affording Bedeschi additional cure time in specified circumstances, including where Bedeschi

 3   commits multiple breaches that Tesla determines have had an aggregate effect comparable to a

 4   material breach. The GTC expressly governs Tesla’s post-termination payment obligations and

 5   provides that Tesla will pay only certain specified amounts, after offsetting amounts due from

 6   Bedeschi for setoffs and liquidated damages. Section 4.4 separately gives Tesla this setoff right

 7   against sums payable to Bedeschi for amounts Tesla determines in good faith that it is owed by

 8   Bedeschi.

 9          The GTC’s dispute-resolution clause provides for JAMS arbitration and gives the arbitrator

10   power to interpret the Contract and fashion appropriate remedies. That grant of authority is

11   expressly limited: the arbitrator has no authority to exceed that of a court having jurisdiction over

12   the parties, no authority to award damages exceeding the types and limitations of damages found

13   in the GTC, and no authority to modify the terms of the GTC.

14          After entering the GTC, the Parties extensively negotiated the terms of Purchase Order #

15   5100460822 (“Purchase Order” or “PO”). As reflected by the Purchase Order, Bedeschi

16   contractually agreed to provide state-of-the-art equipment for a lithium refinery (“Project”), which

17   would be the first lithium refinery in the United States. At the time, Bedeschi was aware and agreed

18   that time was of the essence and that compliance with the Schedule and specifications was

19   paramount. Specifically, after Bedeschi obtained several extensions, the PO required Bedeschi to

20   complete delivery of the Contracted Items by March 1, 2024. After failing to timely deliver Tesla’s

21   equipment under the parties’ contract, Tesla notified Bedeschi that it was in default. When Bedeschi

22   failed to cure, Tesla terminated the PO (but not the GTC).

23          Following the notification of default, Bedeschi improperly raced to the courthouse and, on

24   November 15, 2024, filed a lawsuit against Tesla which attached the PO, making the entire

25   document public in violation of the GTC’s provisions on confidentiality and arbitration. See

26   Plaintiff’s Original Petition Subject to Arbitration Demand, Cause No. 2024-DCV-5004-C, Nueces

27   County, Texas. The same day, Bedeschi filed a Demand for Arbitration.

28
                                                       6
         Case 5:26-cv-07249          Document 1       Filed 07/14/26      Page 7 of 15



 1          Bedeschi initiated arbitration under Section 15.7 of the parties’ January 20, 2023,

 2   agreement. Bedeschi alleged that it furnished engineering services and construction materials for

 3   the Project in and that Tesla had not paid amounts Bedeschi claimed were owed. Tesla

 4   counterclaimed for breach of contract and declaratory relief, including a declaration that Bedeschi’s

 5   lien was invalid and unenforceable and that the lien amount was incorrect.

 6          After a three-day hearing in January 2026 and extensive post-hearing briefing, the

 7   Arbitrator issued an Interim Award on April 30, 2026. The Interim Award found in favor of

 8   Bedeschi on its breach-of-contract claim, awarded Bedeschi significant damages plus pre-award

 9   interest at 1.5% per month under Texas Property Code Chapter 28, declared Bedeschi’s lien valid,

10   denied Tesla all setoffs and counterclaims, and retained jurisdiction for fees and costs. Tesla timely

11   filed objections and a motion for reconsideration identifying material factual and legal errors,

12   including the Award’s conclusion that Tesla terminated the GTC, its use of Texas Property Code §

13   53.286 to void the GTC, its cure and substantial-completion analysis, its denial of setoffs, and its

14   denial of Tesla’s liquidated damages.

15          On July 6, 2026, the Arbitrator issued the Final Award. The Final Award denied Tesla’s

16   objections and motion for reconsideration. The Final Award also granted Bedeschi’s motion for

17   fees and costs, plus conditional fees.

18                                     GROUNDS FOR VACATUR

19          While an arbitrator has broad powers, his discretion is not unlimited. Recognizing this, the

20   Federal Arbitration Act provides grounds for review of an arbitration award. 9 U.S.C. § 10.

21          Under the FAA, a court may vacate an arbitration award, among other reasons, when “the

22   arbitrators exceeded their powers.” 9 U.S.C. § 10(a)(4). In explaining when arbitrators exceed their

23   powers, the Ninth Circuit has held that “[w]hen arbitrators rule on a matter not submitted to them,

24   or act outside the scope of the parties' contractual agreement, the award may be overturned because

25   the arbitrators exceeded the scope of their authority.” Michigan Mut. Ins. Co. v. Unigard Sec. Ins.

26   Co., 44 F.3d 826, 830 (9th Cir. 1995) (citing 9 U.S.C. § 10(a)(4)). The Ninth Circuit has gone on

27   to hold that, under Section 10(a), arbitrators may also “exceed their powers” “not when they merely

28   interpret or apply the governing law incorrectly, but when the award is completely irrational or
                                                        7
           Case 5:26-cv-07249       Document 1       Filed 07/14/26      Page 8 of 15



 1   exhibits a manifest disregard of the law.” Kyocera Corp. v. Prudential-Bache Trade Servs., Inc.,

 2   341 F.3d 987, 997 (9th Cir. 2003) (internal quotations and citations omitted).

 3          To show “manifest disregard of the law,” one must establish that the “arbitrator understood

 4   and correctly stated that law, but proceeded to disregard the same.” Bosack v. Soward, 586 F.3d

 5   1096, 1104 (9th Cir. 2009); see also EHM Prods. v. Starline Tours of Hollywood, Inc., 1 F.4th

 6   1164, 1176 (9th Cir. 2021) (same).

 7          Here, Tesla seeks vacatur because the Award rests on material contradictions and legal

 8   rulings that wholly disregard the terms of the GTC and applicable law, alters the parties’ agreed

 9   remedies, and awards relief beyond the Arbitrator’s delegated authority. As a result, the Award

10   must be vacated.

11   A.     Tesla Never Terminated the GTC; It Terminated the Purchase Order.

12          The Award’s central premise is that “Tesla committed a material breach when it terminated

13   the Contract and then failed to pay Bedeschi the monies it was owed under the Contract [defined

14   as the GTC] just two days later.” Interim Award at 13. This is patently false. The Interim Award

15   itself acknowledges in the “Facts” section that “Tesla terminated the Purchase Order (the most

16   recent revision being from June 27, 2024—PO Rev. 12) for material breach. . . .” Id. at 11. This is

17   consistent with testimony from Tesla’s corporate representative, Willie Hodel, who confirmed this

18   fact: “We terminated the purchase order.” Tr. Vol. 3 at 727:8–10 (“Q: On September 12, 2024, you

19   terminated Bedeschi, correct? A: We terminated the purchase order.”). It is also consistent with the

20   termination letter issued by Tesla in which it states that it “has determined to terminate Purchase

21   Order 5100460822.” In other words, it is clear the Arbitrator understood the distinction between

22   the GTC and the PO—yet he ignored it for purposes of issuing his ruling. This error infects the

23   entire Award.

24          This is not a mere disagreement with the Arbitrator’s weighing of evidence. The Interim

25   Award recognizes the operative fact—that Tesla terminated the Purchase Order—but imposed

26   liability as if Tesla had terminated the GTC instead. That kind of internally contradictory finding

27   on a legally dispositive fact supports vacatur where the fact is so obvious and central that the

28   arbitrator cannot fail to recognize it without manifestly disregarding the law. See Am. Postal
                                                       8
           Case 5:26-cv-07249       Document 1        Filed 07/14/26      Page 9 of 15



 1   Workers Union v. United States Postal Serv., 682 F.2d 1280, 1284–86 (9th Cir. 1982), cert.

 2   denied, 459 U.S. 1200 (1983) (arbitrator’s failure to recognize undisputed, legally dispositive facts

 3   was deemed a manifest disregard for the law). Tesla terminated the PO, not the GTC. So—contrary

 4   to the Award’s ultimate conclusion—Tesla could not have “committed a material breach when it

 5   terminated the [GTC],” and the resulting conclusion that Tesla owes Bedeschi damages cannot

 6   stand. Because the Award’s liability, damages, setoff, lien, and fee determinations flow from this

 7   incorrect premise, the Award exceeds the arbitrator’s powers and should be vacated.

 8   B.     Improper Reliance on the Doctrine of Substantial Performance Alters the GTC.

 9          The Award fails to address the Parties’ contractual agreement that “time [was] of the

10   essence,” instead relying on the inapplicable common-law substantial-performance doctrine. Its

11   application is particularly inappropriate when the parties contracted for a specific post-termination

12   payment regime as they did here. Specifically, Section 12.5(b) of the GTC provides that following

13   termination, Tesla will pay “the applicable portions of the Purchase Price for milestones that Seller

14   successfully achieved prior to the termination date” and “Seller’s actual and reasonable out-of-

15   pocket costs for materials delivered to Tesla.” This is a specific obligation delineated in the GTC.

16   It is not ambiguous and, “absent compelling reasons, courts must respect and enforce the terms of

17   a contract the parties have freely and voluntarily entered.” Pa. Indem. Ins. Co. v. White, 490 S.W.3d

18   468, 471 (Tex. 2016).

19          The Award did not enforce the formula prescribed by the GTC and agreed to by the Parties.

20   Instead, the Arbitrator invoked the common-law doctrine of substantial performance and held that,

21   because Bedeschi substantially completed its work, Bedeschi was entitled to the entire unpaid

22   contract price. The Award even acknowledged Tesla’s argument that Section 12.5(b) limited any

23   recovery to milestones successfully achieved and out-of-pocket costs, but then completely ignored

24   it. For reasons discussed below, that is wrong. But more critically for this request for vacatur, that

25   approach rewrites Section 12.5(b) by converting a milestone-by-milestone, offset-sensitive

26   payment clause into a common-law full-price remedy. In other words, the Arbitrator unilaterally

27   overwrote a bargained-for allocation and modified critical terms of the GTC, which Section 15.7(c)

28
                                                        9
         Case 5:26-cv-07249         Document 1       Filed 07/14/26      Page 10 of 15



 1   expressly forbids: the arbitrator “will not have any right or authority . . . to modify the terms of

 2   either the Contract or these General Terms.” GTC § 15.7(c).

 3          Not only did the Arbitrator violate the express terms of the GTC when he modified the post-

 4   termination payment obligations, the doctrine was not properly applied and the analysis fails on its

 5   own terms, despite the Arbitrator’s clear awareness of the proper framework which he then chose

 6   to disregard. The Award stated that substantial completion entitles a contractor to the contract price

 7   less offsets for remediable defects. For example, under the substantial completion doctrine, the

 8   burden was on Bedeschi to establish and present evidence on how much it would reasonably cost

 9   to complete the parts of the contract that remained to be completed (because it is understood that

10   the contract was only substantially complete, not actually complete), and the cost to remedy any

11   defects in Bedeschi’s existing work. Though he was aware of Bedeschi’s legal burden, the

12   Arbitrator improperly shifted the burden to Tesla to prove the offsets, remedy the defects, and

13   establish the cost to complete the contract. The Award specifically notes that “Tesla did not meet

14   its burden of proving it was entitled to any offsets.” But the burden under the law is Bedeschi’s,

15   and the Arbitrator ignored it, improperly placing the burden to prove any offsets, remedy any

16   defects, and the cost to complete the contract on Tesla, which he then incorrectly concludes Tesla

17   failed to do. Contrary to the Award and even though the burden under the theory in the Award

18   should have been Bedeschi’s, Tesla proved multiple defects under Tesla’s own theories of relief,

19   which were required to be offset:

20          Milestones 5 and 6 were never achieved. The Contract’s payment structure required six

21   milestones. It is undisputed that Milestone 5 (completed delivery of equipment free of defects and

22   liens) and Milestone 6 (site acceptance testing and run rate) were not completed. Hodel testified

23   Milestone 5 required equipment “delivered without defect and without liens” and confirmed it “was

24   not complete” before termination. See Tr. Vol. 2 at 478:10-16. Site acceptance testing—requiring

25   95% availability over a period of 14 consecutive production days—similarly did not occur. See id.

26   at 480:10-14. That evidence was never contradicted.

27          Documented equipment defects. Hodel identified significant defects, including but not

28   limited to: bucket elevator and belt conveyor issues (detailed in the Hargrove report), a backwards-
                                                       10
         Case 5:26-cv-07249         Document 1        Filed 07/14/26      Page 11 of 15



 1   designed gearbox causing leaks, and multiple conveyor sections with quality issues causing major

 2   construction downtime. See Tr. Vol. 3 at 549:8-558:17; id. at 570:20-575:5; id. at 577:25-578:12;

 3   id. at 581:15-582:8. The Award never addressed this evidence. Substantial completion requires the

 4   owner receive the “object of their contract”; non-functional equipment is not that object.

 5          The “95% complete” assertion was self-serving and unverified. The Arbitrator credited

 6   Bedeschi’s July 10, 2024, email claiming “over 95% complete” and faulted Tesla for not

 7   responding to “refute or reject this assertion.” But there is no contractual obligation to respond to a

 8   vendor’s self-assessment of completion. Silence is not acceptance under the GTC and the Arbitrator

 9   improperly shifted the burden to Tesla to disprove Bedeschi’s own self-serving claim when it had

10   no obligation to do so. Even if the Arbitrator accepted Bedeschi’s claim as true, that still leaves 5%

11   of the work that would have needed to be completed, and for which Bedeschi should have been

12   made to establish the cost to complete, to be entitled to any award under the substantial completion

13   doctrine. Despite being aware of this requirement, the Arbitrator simply disregarded this burden

14   and left it unaddressed.

15          The Ninth Circuit has vacated an award where the arbitrator recognized contractual

16   requirements but avoided them because enforcing them seemed unfair. As the Ninth Circuit has

17   held, “[w]hen an arbitrator disregards the plain text of a contract without legal justification simply

18   to reach a result that he believes is just,” judicial intervention is required. Aspic Eng’g & Constr.

19   Co. v. ECC Centcom Constructors, LLC, 913 F.3d 1162, 1169 (9th Cir. 2019); see also Pacific

20   Motor Trucking Co. v. Automotive Machinists Union, 702 F.2d 176 (9th Cir. 1983). In this case,

21   judicial intervention is required because the Arbitrator chose to forgo contractual enforcement in

22   favor of something he believed to be fairer to Bedeschi. The Award recognized Section 12.5(b) and

23   recognized Tesla’s setoff provisions, but the Arbitrator displaced those provisions with a common-

24   law gap-filler remedy and broad equitable payment result despite the express limits on his power.

25   This Court should vacate the award as a result.

26

27

28
                                                        11
           Case 5:26-cv-07249       Document 1        Filed 07/14/26      Page 12 of 15



 1   C.      The Texas Property Code Does Not Void the GTC, and the Finding is Entirely

 2           Unsupported.

 3           The Award states that “section 14 [Confidential Information] of the GTCs is void as a matter

 4   of law under Texas Property Code section 53.286” because it is overbroad as it “would not allow

 5   Bedeschi to file or enforce a lien without being in violation of that section.” In essence, the

 6   Arbitrator contended that, when filing a lien, “Bedeschi would be required to include information

 7   that section 14 explicitly prohibits from disclosing.” The Award is the first ever in any jurisdiction

 8   in the country that purports to rely on Section 53.286 of the Texas Property Code to void an

 9   agreement. There is no record—and Bedeschi has implicitly conceded there is no record—of any

10   court in any jurisdiction supporting the Arbitrator’s use of Section 53.286.

11           Pointedly, the Arbitrator violated clearly established law. Section 53.286 voids only

12   agreements “purporting to waive the right to file or enforce any lien . . . .” Tex. Prop. Code § 53.286

13   (emphasis added). Nothing in the GTC purports to waive Bedeschi’s right to file a lien under

14   Chapter 53 and Bedeschi did not identify any such provision. Nor does the language of the GTC

15   conflict with Bedeschi’s obligations to provide certain information under the Property Code.

16           During the Arbitration, Hodel specifically testified that a lien that did not contain the PO or

17   specific contract terms did not violate Section 14.2. See Tr. Vol. 3 at 597:13–18. He also testified

18   that other contractors have filed liens that did not attach a PO or GTC terms, and Tesla did not

19   assert that was a violation of confidentiality. Id. at 604:11–15. While a lien claimant may attach a

20   copy of a written agreement in support of its claim, the use of “may” shows this is optional and not

21   required. Tex. Prop. Code § 53.054(b). As such, Bedeschi could—and did—file a lien when it

22   initiated a lawsuit in Nueces County, Texas. That right was not waived. Tesla has never once argued

23   that the GTC precluded those filings. And for good reason—it does not.

24           What Tesla did contend is a separate and distinct challenge to Bedeschi’s filings that do not

25   implicate any alleged waiver: Tesla maintains that Bedeschi was not required to, and should not

26   have, filed the entire PO in the public record, as it disclosed far more information than required by

27   law to enforce its lien, and it was that specific disclosure violated Bedeschi’s promise to maintain

28   confidentiality. The Arbitrator, however, acting in a novel and draconian fashion, relied on Texas
                                                        12
           Case 5:26-cv-07249       Document 1        Filed 07/14/26       Page 13 of 15



 1   Property Code Section 53.054 to void the parties’ agreement. The Arbitrator well exceeded his

 2   authority by taking the statute far beyond any previous or supported use to void the parties’ express

 3   and unambiguous agreement, and his decision should be vacated.

 4   D.      Unrecoverable Costs, Expenses, and Conditional Appellate Fees Were Awarded.

 5           Proceeding on an Award riddled with fundamental legal and factual errors, the Arbitrator

 6   nonetheless granted attorneys’ fees and costs, treating Bedeschi as the “prevailing party.” Further

 7   compounding his previous errors, the Arbitrator resolved to award Bedeschi substantial costs that

 8   are not recoverable under Texas law or the GTC.

 9           Section 15.7(c) provides that each party bears its own expenses and shares arbitration costs,

10   while allowing the arbitrator discretion to award reasonable costs and fees to the prevailing party.

11   The clause does not authorize expert-witness fees, mediation fees, catering, witness travel, hotel

12   stays, meals, legal research, copying charges, or conditional future fees untethered to services

13   actually incurred.

14           In Texas, taxable costs are awarded to the prevailing party unless a statute, rule, or court

15   order provides otherwise. See Tex. R. Civ. P. 131. “‘Costs’ usually refers to fees and charges

16   required by law to be paid to the courts or some of their officers, the amount of which is fixed by

17   statute or the court’s rules, for example filing and service fees.” Hatfield v. Solomon, 316 S.W.3d

18   50, 66 (Tex. App.—Houston [14th Dist.] 2010, no pet.) (quoting Sterling Bank v. Willard M, L.L.C.,

19   221 S.W.3d 121, 124 (Tex. App.—Houston [1st Dist.] 2006, no pet.)). Taxable costs do not include

20   attorney’s fees and generally only encompass “relatively minor, incidental expenses” that make up

21   a small portion of a party’s total expenses in a case. See Taniguchi v. Kan Pac. Saipan, Ltd., 566

22   U.S. 560, 573 (2012).

23           Several Texas rules and statutes further clarify what is included in the category of

24   recoverable taxable costs. For example, Section 31.007 of the Texas Civil Practice and Remedies

25   Code allows the following costs in a party’s recovery: (1) fees of the clerk and service fees due the

26   county; (2) fees of the court reporter for the original of stenographic transcripts necessarily obtained

27   for use in the suit; (3) masters, interpreters, and guardians ad litem appointed pursuant to these rules

28   and state statutes; and (4) such other costs and fees as may be permitted by these rules and state
                                                        13
         Case 5:26-cv-07249         Document 1         Filed 07/14/26      Page 14 of 15



 1   statutes. Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 31.007(b). Similarly, Rule 203.2 allows a clerk to tax as

 2   costs the “deposition officer’s charges for preparing the original deposition transcript” but not a

 3   copy. Tex. R. Civ. P. 203.2; Tex. R. Civ. P. 140. In other words, not all expenses are recoverable

 4   as costs, but the arbitrator rejected these limits imposed by law. The Final Award concluded that

 5   “costs” in the GTC was not limited to taxable costs and encompassed all reasonable costs incurred

 6   in the arbitration.

 7           In support of his decision, the Arbitrator relied on an inapplicable federal case that does not

 8   discuss the limitations on costs and is based on an entirely different set of rules from the ones the

 9   parties agreed to enforce. Specifically, the Arbitrator claimed that Texas law authorizes him to

10   impose “any remedy that is permitted under applicable law; provided, however, that the arbitrator

11   may not award any remedies that the parties have agreed in writing may not be awarded in

12   arbitration.” That language, however, is not “Texas law,” it is very specifically—as described in

13   the single case cited by the Arbitrator—the “Better Business Bureau’s Rule of Arbitration 3.”

14   Apollo Companies, Inc. v. Mem’l Vill. Emergency Room, LLC, No. 14-24-00589-CV, 2025 WL

15   1232066, at *7 (Tex. App.—Houston [14th Dist.] Apr. 29, 2025, pet. denied).

16           Plainly, there is no authority allowing the Arbitrator to waver from the technical definition

17   of costs to include nonrecoverable expenses and conditional fees yet unproven as part of the Award.

18   Despite his lack of authority to grant these costs and fees, the Arbitrator awarded them, noting that

19   he is permitted to award “any remedy” under the Better Business Bureau’s dispute resolution rule,

20   which he erroneously attributes to “Texas law,” while simultaneously failing to recognize that the

21   term “costs” carries a technical meaning defined by various rules and statutes. This is a clear

22   overreach of his authority, and the Award must be vacated. Likewise, the Arbitrator relied on a

23   facially deficient lawyer declaration in awarding conditional appellate fees that plainly did not

24   comply with Texas law.

25                                     CONCLUSION AND PRAYER

26           The Final Award should be vacated because the Arbitrator exceeded his authority as

27   described herein, the Court also should award Tesla its costs and attorneys’ fees incurred in

28   pursuing this Petition, and award Tesla all other relief to which it is entitled.
